Major powers are directly involved in conflicts , support one side in ongoing wars , or prevent collective action . The problem , therefore , is not the absence of diplomatic capacity or the lack of treaties and institutions . The deeper issue is that the intellectual frameworks guiding international conduct are no longer adequate for the challenges before us . <h> A crisis of frameworks <p> The crisis that confronts the world is not merely geopolitical . It is civilisational . The dominant frameworks of power politics that shaped international relations in recent decades are failing to provide a pathway toward stability . In such moments , the search for alternative intellectual traditions becomes important . <p> India offers one such tradition . This contribution does not arise from India 's position as an emerging power , seeking greater influence in global institutions . Its significance lies in the civilisational ideas that have shaped Indian thought for several millennia and that continue to remain part of its intellectual heritage . <p> During India 's presidency of the G20 in 2023 , Prime @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kutumbakam -- One Earth , One Family , One Future . The New Delhi Declaration articulated a set of commitments anchored in four principles -- People , Planet , Prosperity , and Peace . These principles were presented in the language of contemporary policy , but their conceptual roots lie deep within India 's civilisational tradition . <p> The Dharmic tradition identifies four foundational aims of human life -- Dharma , Artha , Kama and Moksha . These principles are usually discussed in relation to individual conduct and spiritual evolution . Yet they also represent a framework for organising social and political life . When viewed through this lens , the four priorities articulated in the New Delhi declaration align with these classical ideas with striking clarity . <p> Dharma represents the principle that action must be governed by ethical restraint and responsibility . It establishes that power must operate within limits . The rules-based international order that emerged after World War II was an imperfect attempt to translate this idea into the language of international law . It assumed that even powerful nations would operate within a framework of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ under strain . Powerful states increasingly justify unilateral military action and territorial assertion . The result is the weakening of the very principles that once constrained conflict . When the normative foundation erodes , the system loses its capacity to regulate behaviour . <p> The erosion of Dharma leads inevitably to instability in Artha . Economic prosperity that is disconnected from justice can not remain stable . The economic consequences of recent conflicts illustrate this clearly . Disruptions in energy supply , rising inflation , and threats to food security have begun to affect countries far removed from the battlefields themselves . When prosperity is pursued without ethical restraint , it begins to undermine its own foundations . <p> The third dimension involves Kama , understood as human desire . Desire in itself is not condemned within the Dharmic tradition . It becomes destructive only when it escapes the limits imposed by Dharma . @@135473817 <h> Religious Liberty at Risk : The Costs of State-Enabled Islamophobia <p> The International Day to Combat Islamophobia arrived this year as the United States and Israel deepened military confrontation with Iran -- an atmosphere that has pushed anti-Muslim rhetoric from the margins into mainstream Western politics . In the United States , several recent statements by elected officials have raised alarms among civil rights advocates , constitutional scholars , and interfaith leaders who warn that such language is incompatible with democratic norms and the First Amendment 's guarantee of religious freedom . These concerns are not abstract : history shows that when governments normalize suspicion or hostility toward a religious minority , the consequences can be profound and long-lasting . <p> That danger is visible again today , as remarks by President Donald Trump and several Republican lawmakers illustrate how deeply Islamophobia has become entangled with national politics . In a radio interview , Trump attributed recent violent incidents to the " genetics " of alleged assailants , suggesting that some people " should n't have been let in " and that " something is wrong there . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and at a synagogue in Michigan , the latter involving a U.S. citizen of Lebanese origin whose family had recently been killed in an Israeli strike . Experts have long associated such references to " genetics " with racial pseudoscience and eugenics , which modern science has rejected as unethical and discriminatory . The inconsistency speaks for itself : when a white American shot the president during the election campaign , " genetics " never entered the conversation . It surfaces only when the suspect can be othered . That is not science -- it is scapegoating dressed up as biology . <p> Trump 's rhetoric has coincided with a surge of openly anti-Muslim statements from members of Congress . Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee declared that " Muslims do n't belong in American society , " calling pluralism " a lie . " In a speech last year , he said that " America is and must always be a Christian nation . " Other lawmakers have echoed similar sentiments . " No more Muslims immigrating to America , " posted Rep. Brandon Gill , R-Texas on Thursday . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more Islamophobia , not less , " while Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama posted a photo of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks side-by-side with a photo of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is Muslim . The caption read : " The enemy is inside the gates . " These statements have drawn condemnation from Democrats and civil rights groups . " Islamophobia is a cancer that must be eradicated from both the Congress and the Country . The intent is unmistakable : invoking this imaginary threat as a political boogeyman is meant to scare the public and legitimize hostility toward an entire religious community . <p> The United States has confronted this dynamic in earlier wars . In World War II @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a narrative that helped justify internment and the destruction of civilian populations . Historians have long observed that powerful states often rely on racialized rhetoric to make their wars appear necessary or inevitable . The language now used to describe Muslims in Gaza , Lebanon , and Iran follows this familiar script of dehumanization : entire communities are portrayed as inherently dangerous , lowering the moral threshold for military action . <p> According to reporting from ABC News , this pattern reflects a broader rise in anti-Muslim rhetoric among Republican lawmakers , particularly in the context of the ongoing war involving Iran . Analysts note that the shift marks a departure from earlier periods when party leaders more consistently condemned such language . <p> History offers sobering examples of what happens when governments legitimize hostility toward a religious minority . In the United States , anti-Catholic sentiment in the 19th century fueled violence , discriminatory laws , and political movements such as the Know-Nothing Party . Anti-Jewish rhetoric in Europe during the early 20th century laid the groundwork for exclusionary policies that escalated into catastrophic violence . More recently , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ against Muslims and those perceived to be Muslim , including Sikhs and Arab-Americans . Civil rights organizations documented widespread surveillance , profiling , and detentions that disproportionately targeted Muslim communities . <p> These episodes demonstrate a consistent pattern : when political leaders frame a minority group as inherently suspect , foreign , or dangerous , public hostility increases , legal protections erode , and violence becomes more likely . The state 's role -- whether through explicit policy or permissive silence -- can either restrain or accelerate these dynamics . <p> One of the most striking contrasts between the present moment and the aftermath of 9/11 is the role of presidential leadership . In 2001 , President George W. Bush visited a mosque within days of the attacks , and declared , " Islam is peace . " " Those who feel like they can intimidate our fellow citizens to take out their anger do n't represent the best of America , " Bush said . That message , delivered from the highest office in the country , helped prevent an already volatile situation from spiraling further . <p> Today @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Maya Berry of the Arab American Institute , the current climate is " worse than what we saw post-9/11 " because the presidential " bully pulpit " is being used not to calm tensions but to amplify suspicion . Hate-crime data reflect this shift : the largest spike in anti-Muslim and anti-Arab hate crimes occurred after 9/11 , but the second-largest spike came during the 2015 -- 2016 period , coinciding with the rise of Trump 's initial presidential campaign . The pattern suggests that political rhetoric has a measurable impact on public behavior . <p> The United States is not the only country witnessing a rise in Islamophobia . Across Western Europe , anti-Muslim sentiment has been fueled by decades of migration from regions once colonized or occupied by European powers . @@135473827 <p> Geopolitics in capitalism is greatly shaped by energy and raw material availability , technology , production systems , finance and markets . Of these factors , energy plays a central role . Power in 2025 flows through pipelines , transmission lines , shipping lanes , semiconductor cleanrooms , digital networks , and financial institutions . The states that command these systems will control the immediate future . <p> The rivalry between the United States and China is fundamentally about control of technology , production systems and markets . Russia 's war in Ukraine reveals how energy markets are weaponised . The Middle East demonstrates the enduring centrality of oil even in an energy transition . <p> Capitalism has failed to solve the problems of inequality and sustainability . Fossil fuels and 80 critical non-renewables will be exhausted before 2100 . None of the renewable energy sources can completely replace fossil fuels . The energy transition from fossil fuels to renewables has been sluggish . Global warming is out of control and threatens to overwhelm society before this century end . <p> Many civilisations in the past have collapsed due to energy collapses . Capitalism today faces the same prospect , and this collapse will be global . The only solution is for the world to power down and agree on an equitable regime for the use of energy and other raw materials . <p> ENERGY PRIMER <p> Primacy of Energy <p> Energy is the mover and shaker of all processes in the universe . Without the play of energy , the universe will be in a dead state , and all processes , abiotic and biotic , will come to a dead halt . Natural history is the study of how energy flows shaped the evolution of the universe . <p> All life forms require energy for their survival . Species other than humans take only as much energy as they require for their survival and reproduction , the latter requiring only a small fraction of the total energy used by the species . <p> Humans have the ability to understand how energy has shaped nature ( science ) . Humans used energy to extract raw materials and fashion them into goods and services ( technology ) . No other species on earth can do this . Over time , scientific and technological knowledge grew . In the last three centuries , growth was exponential , as was the harvest of energy and raw materials to produce goods and services . <p> Social history is the description of how human society has changed over time in its working and structure , consequent to the use of an increasing amount of energy and raw materials to make and consume artefacts and services , thereby altering the environment . <p> EROEI <p> All land and water produce energy as photosynthesis occurs amidst them . Some lands and water bodies are better endowed geologically and climatically to produce energy , e.g. , fertile valleys and estuaries in tropical countries , and consequently have greater biodiversity , support higher human populations , and have older civilisations . <p> Energy from photosynthesis is in the form of food and fuel , and material in the form of fibre and wood . Other large available energy sources are : animate ( animal and human ) , fossil fuels , wind , solar , geothermal , wave and tide , gravitational , and nuclear energy . Harvesting energy from any energy source , including solar energy , requires an energy input . For example , for obtaining fossil fuels , energy is required for prospecting , extracting , transporting , and sometimes refining them . Harvesting food crops using solar energy requires preparing a field and inputting other necessities . <p> The ratio of the energy obtained from an energy source to the energy invested to obtain it is known as the EROEI ( Energy Return on Energy Invested ) . The higher the EROEI of an energy source , the lower the energy cost per unit of energy , and the greater the ease and preference of obtaining it . Energy from fossil fuels has a higher EROEI than biofuels and is therefore preferred to the latter . <p> EROEI of an energy source can increase with technology upgrades . For example , farm technology improvements in the early and middle ages increased the EROEI of food crops . However , the EROEI of an energy source may drop if it becomes harder to obtain . The EROEI of coal was as high as 80 in the early 20th Century but dropped to 20-30 in the 21st Century as it became harder to get to coal seams . <p> Surplus Energy -- Generation , Acquisition , Accumulation <p> If 1 Joule ( J ) of energy is spent to produce oil ( EROEI = 20 ) , the investor of that energy obtains oil containing 20 J , 19 of which is surplus energy . The generation of surplus energy occurs because the harvested energy contains considerably more energy than the energy invested to obtain it . <p> Social development is possible only if there is surplus energy . Surplus energy is one of the material bases for the economic categories of surplus value , profit and capital . No other species on earth can create surplus energy . <p> By virtue of having invested 1 J , the investor acquires the entire harvested energy , i.e. , 20 J. S/he then claims ownership of all the energy s/he has acquired , including the surplus energy of 19 J. <p> Out of the 20 J , if s/he now invests 2 J to produce more oil , s/he will get 40 J worth of oil through the same technology , i.e. of identical EROEI , of which 38 J is surplus energy . The investor now accumulates surplus energy that can be converted into capital or wealth . <p> The process is similar to investments of monetary capital in the production process that leads to the generation of profit in monetary form . This process can go on ad infinitum under the capitalist production system . Here , this surplus energy obtained in the sphere of production can be exchanged in the market to be converted into monetary form , or capital stock or wealth . The UN System of Environmental Economic Accounting recognises this and treats energy ( and other natural resources ) at par with physical capital . <p> Embodied Energy <p> The energy required to produce a product or service in the entire supply chain is known as its embodied energy . In this way , the ' value ' of a good or service is proportional to its embodied energy . For example , a car is more expensive than a cycle because a cycle requires more raw materials and energy . Embodied energy that has the potential to help generate more embodied energy ( means of production ) is one of the material bases for the generation of surplus energy , as the energy invested to harvest an energy source includes embodied energy in the form of machinery , etc. ( means of production ) . In the above example , 1 J includes the flow of energy , such as electricity , the energy to produce the coal that produced the electricity and so on , besides the depreciation in the ' value ' of the machine that was used in the process of producing 20 J of oil . <p> Acquiring and Accumulating Surplus through Conquest and Colonialism <p> Since ancient times , the conquest and colonising of alien lands was a way to seize raw materials and surplus energy in the form of crops and capture embodied energy in the form of wealth and artefacts , and subjugate humans from the conquered territory to create additional food crops and artefacts for further and subsequent appropriations . <p> In 1532 , Spanish marauder Pizarro captured the Inca emperor , Atahuallpa , by defeating his 80,000-strong army with just 168 horse-mounted Spaniard soldiers with cannons , muskets , steel spears and swords , and wearing chainmail armour . Superior knowledge of metallurgy and horses gave the Spaniards an advantage &amp; to extract the largest ransom ever . <p> In the 200 years between the mid-18th and 20th centuries , vast areas of Asia , America and Africa , having about a third of the world 's population was colonised by European powers . The colonial powers usurped a massive amount of surplus generated in these continents . <p> Vasco de Gama landed in Calicut in 1498 . China , India and the Arabs had ships that were as good as or better than European ships . European ships had a stern post rudder that gave them maneuverability , a mix of different types of sails on their three masts that gave them greater speed , and strongly built hulls that made them capable of withstanding more punishment . In sea battles , soon after the Europeans landed in India , they were able to outmaneuver Indian ships and outgun them , as the Indians had not yet mastered the use of ship-mounted cannons despite possessing them . The Europeans soon extracted tribute from the Indians and the Arabs for using the sea lanes . <p> In the last 3 centuries , colonial powers -- British , Dutch , and French were able to extract huge energy surpluses in the form of raw materials , and by producing goods in offshore factories that had low costs . The British Empire thrived because it was able to harvest energy resources from its vast colonies in both the old and the new worlds . <p> Acquiring and Accumulating Surplus through Unequal Exchange <p> The sunlight energy that contributes to photosynthesis in crops is not valued , whereas energy inputs , e.g. , fossil fuels and electricity that contribute to the production of agro inputs , e.g. , farm machinery , agrochemicals , are priced and their price contributes to the cost of farm machinery . However , in energy equations of farm produce , energy in sunlight is considered as an input energy , which then contributes to the energy content of the farm produce . <p> This results in an anomaly between the economic equation and the energy equation for farm produce . In the economic equation , the sun 's contribution is not considered , as it is costless , while in the energy equation , it is captured . This allows the industry sector to do an unequal exchange of energy with the agricultural sector , hence monetarily benefiting . The harvesting of any energy source has an energy cost . In the case of fossil fuels , the cost of fossil fuels is the price paid for prospecting , extracting , transporting and refining them . In the case of sunlight that goes into crops , energy is expended to prepare land for the crops , etc , which is not counted . <p> The agriculture sector is at a permanent disadvantage vis- ? -vis the industrial sector , as there is unequal exchange of energy between these sectors . In short , among the various ' value additions ' taking place in the agricultural sector , only those that are attributed to labour and machinery are counted for in the economic equation . Likewise , the Global South that exchanges crops for industrial products from the Global North is in an unequal exchange of energy with the latter . Hence , continuous to remain backward in comparison to the Global North . <p> Bourgeoises Economics Encourages Unsustainability and Inequality <p> By not costing sunlight , which is a sustainable source of energy and costing fossil fuels and nuclear energy , economics encourages unsustainability . Fossil fuels and nuclear energy are unsustainable , as fossil fuels will be exhausted in about 100 years , and uranium ore in about 150 years . However , since fossil fuels and nuclear energy are costed , these forms of energy are preferred to solar energy as they will add value and fetch the products and services using them a higher price than if solar energy is used , hence will be preferred over solar energy . <p> Energy and Carbon Inequality <p> Private ownership of surplus energy and embodied energy in the means of production , conquest of territories , colonialism and unequal exchange because sunlight is not costed , whereas other energy sources are costed , has led to a significant gap in the per capita energy consumption between and within capitalist countries . This reflects in the gap between income and wealth between the rich and the poor -- nations and people . The per capita energy consumption in various countries and regions is given in the table below . <p> Carbon inequality reflects the same pattern as energy inequality . The rich emit significantly more per capita CO2 than the poor , and are therefore responsible for global warming . <p> Who Owns Surplus and Embodied Energy ? <p> Surplus energy and embodied energy may be owned privately , jointly , collectively , by the state or a legal person such as a corporation or an association . In hunting-gathering societies , the small amount of surplus and embodied energy was held collectively . In a class society , slavery , feudalism , capitalism , surplus , and embodied energy are largely privately owned . In socialism , they are socially owned , but held largely by the state . In communism , it is envisaged that they will be held socially . <p> The question to ask is how much energy was expended to make oil that yields 1 J of energy , and who expended the invested energy . The answer is nature . Nature baked dead biota at high temperatures in its crust for 300 million years to make fossil fuels . <p> The energy that nature used to make fossil fuels is many orders of magnitude more than the 1 J invested to acquire ( prospect , extract , transport , and refine ) fossil fuels from nature . The embodied energy is fossil fuels is ancient sunlight . So , who should fossil fuels belong to -- nature or the humans who acquired them ? <p> Human Labour is an Energy Conversion Process <p> Human labour is an energy conversion process similar to a heat engine , like a prime mover . Likewise , the economy is also a heat engine . Energy is therefore a more basic category than labour , and more useful to understand the exploitation of nature by humans and that of the working class by the bourgeoisie . <p> The economy also does energy conversion and therefore should be treated as a heat engine to understand its working . <p> Mode of Production <p> The manner in which surplus energy is generated , acquired and accumulated is the same in all modes of class societies -- slavery , feudalism and capitalism . The form in which surplus is generated , acquired and accumulated varies in each mode . The mode of production debate that occurred a few decades back looked only at the form and not at the process of surplus generation , acquisition and accumulation . <p> ENERGY IN HISTORY <p> Energy , not money , ideas or institutions , is the fundamental driver of social change . Across millennia , the scale , density , and efficiency of energy capture have shaped population size , economic output , political organisation , and technological complexity . Without changes in energy regimes , major civilizational shifts would have been impossible . Human progress is best understood as a succession of energy transitions . <p> Hunting-Gathering Societies <p> In hunter-gatherer societies , the energy used was limited to human power and biomass , i.e. , wood . The daily energy budget of individuals depended on food gathering and hunting , constraining population densities to very low levels . Because energy flows were small and diffuse , social organisation remained relatively egalitarian and mobile . Such societies were efficient within their ecological niches but incapable of supporting large cities , standing armies , or complex states . For example , Palaeolithic communities relied entirely on muscle power for hunting large animals and on wood fires for cooking -- an energy regime that limited surplus production and thus restricted social stratification . <p> Agricultural Societies <p> The transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture that occurred about 10,000 years ago was marked by a profound increase in usable energy . By domesticating plants and animals , humans began appropriating a far larger share of photosynthetic output . Fields of wheat or rice concentrated solar energy into storable grain , while domesticated cattle and horses multiplied human mechanical power . This shift dramatically raised human population densities and enabled permanent settlements . Early agrarian civilisations in Mesopotamia , China and India are examples of how irrigation and animal traction expanded energy capture beyond what human muscles alone could achieve . <p> Animal power in particular represented a decisive amplification of work capacity . A single ox could deliver several times the sustained power of a human labourer , making large-scale plough agriculture feasible . In medieval Europe , the heavy plough and horse collar improved energy efficiency in farming , allowing cultivation of heavier soils and boosting yields . Though biomass -- wood for heating , charcoal for metallurgy -- remained central to human existence , agricultural societies commanded layered energy flows : human , animal , and plant-based . These surpluses supported cities , specialised crafts , bureaucracies , and imperial states . <p> Agrarian civilisations were ultimately constrained by the limits of photosynthesis . Land area capped energy availability ; deforestation and soil depletion often followed demographic growth . Pre-industrial societies repeatedly approached ecological ceilings . For example , late imperial China and early modern Europe faced wood shortages and pressure on arable land . Economic expansion without new energy sources led to stagnation . And many early civilisations collapsed , and not just stagnated , due to their inability to locate new energy sources , or ways to improve the EROI for the existing sources . <p> Industrial Societies <p> In the transition to industrial society , coal was the first transformative fossil fuel . During the 18th and 19th-centuries , coal replaced wood as the primary source of heat and power in Britain first and subsequently in Europe and later in the rest of the world . The steam engine converted coal 's chemical energy into mechanical motion , liberating industry from reliance on animate , biomass , wind , and water energies . Fossil fuels offered energy densities far beyond traditional biomass , enabling sustained and high economic growth . <p> One example of this transformation is the replacement of charcoal with coke in iron smelting . This innovation dramatically increased steel production , supporting railways , ships , and urban infrastructure . Another is the expansion of rail transport , which multiplied the speed and scale of trade by harnessing coal-fired locomotives . These developments were not merely technological ; they reshaped social organisation , urbanisation patterns , and global trade networks . <p> Oil and natural gas further intensified the fossil-fuel era in the 20th Century . Oil 's high energy density and portability made it ideal for internal combustion engines , revolutionising transportation and warfare . Natural gas improved heating efficiency and became a key feedstock for fertiliser production , boosting agricultural yields through synthetic nitrogen . Modern civilisation -- from skyscrapers to global aviation -- rests fundamentally on fossil energy flows . <p> Energy availability determines the scale of economies , the complexity of institutions , and the capacity for technological innovation . From the muscle-powered bands of hunter-gatherers to fossil-fuelled industrial societies , each leap in energy capture has enabled new forms of social organisation . Without energy transitions , there would have been no agricultural revolutions , no industrialisation , and no modern world . <p> NATION-STATES ' RIGHTS TO DRAW ENERGY FROM THEIR TERRITORY <p> Geopolitics is the interaction between nation-states to assert and defend their rights over territories , or to capture or colonise other states or territories . It is , therefore , important to understand the meaning of a state and a nation , the difference between the two and how they became a hyphenated phrase . Nation-states today jockey for power and influence by cooperating with friendly nation-states and conflicting with others that are deemed unfriendly . This is the essence of geopolitics , and the acquisition and control of energy is at the centre of it . <p> Borders <p> Human-drawn borders , i.e. , other than ecological , geological and climatic ones , demarcate a territory or a space for an individual , a village , a collective , an organisation , a state , or a union of countries . Within this territory , the above entities may acquire the right to harvest , use , and extract raw materials such as energy , water , and other renewable and non-renewable materials . The entity may claim ownership over the territory or may lease it . Entities may defend their rights over the territory either by law or otherwise . <p> States <p> Modern society is built upon the idea of the nation-state , a political form that emerged unevenly across regions but eventually became universal in the 20th Century . States existed in early and medieval times in the form of empires based on imperial law ( Roman ) , dynastic monarchies ( Mauryan , Tang , Sahelian ) , religious-imperial ( Aztec , Inca ) , or city-states ( Hellenic ) . <p> After the 1648 " Peace of Westphalia " treaties were signed in Munster and Osnabr ? ck in Germany , the sovereign state was defined as : having political authority over a geographic area with defined territorial borders , being formally equal in diplomacy to other sovereign states , having the right to no interference in its internal affairs by other states , having the right to negotiate treaties directly with other sovereign states . The treaties ended two major wars in Europe , diminished the authority of the Roman Catholic Church over European kingdoms , and brought order to kingdoms that were a jumble of multi-ethnic territories without clear national borders . <p> The 1993 Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States extends the definition of a sovereign state as having a geographically defined territory with a permanent population with an effective government capable of exercising authority over its territory and entering into relationships with other states independently . <p> The state is a political and legal organisation that exercises authority over a defined territory and population . A state typically possesses institutions such as a government , legal system , military , and administrative bureaucracy . <p> Nations <p> A nation is different from a state . It refers to a community of people who perceive themselves as sharing a common identity based on language , culture , history , territory , or collective memory . A nation is primarily a cultural and psychological community , not necessarily a political one . A nation can exist without political sovereignty , as seen historically in groups like the Kurds spread across several Middle Eastern states , or indigenous populations in various countries . <p> In the 19th Century , nationalism spread across the world , becoming a powerful force in movements for political unification , independence , and self-determination . <p> Nation-State <p> The relationship between nation and state gave rise to the concept of the nation-state , where the boundaries of the political state roughly coincide with the boundaries of a nation . Ideally , a nation-state exists when a culturally unified people govern themselves within a sovereign territory . In practice , however , few states perfectly match this ideal . Many states contain multiple national or ethnic groups , while some nations remain divided across several states . <p> The merging of the nation ( a cultural community ) and the state ( a political entity with sovereignty over a territory ) was historically a gradual process that unfolded between the 17th and 20th centuries in an uneven way across the world . Several major developments -- political , economic , and cultural -- brought the two together to form the modern nation-state . <p> Before the modern era , most states were dynastic empires or kingdoms , where loyalty was to a ruler rather than to the people of the state . The turning point came during the French Revolution with the emergence of the idea that political authority belongs to the people , and not to monarchs , and the concept of the nation was linked to political sovereignty , i.e. , the state . <p> During the 19th Century , governments increasingly undertook nation-building projects to create a unified national identity within their territories , involving standardising national languages , expanding mass schooling and literacy , promoting national histories , myths , and symbols , and creating national armies and bureaucracies . Through these institutions , states actively constructed national identity . <p> Nationalist movements also worked in the opposite direction : instead of states creating nations , nations sought states . In the 19th Century , nationalist movements unified fragmented territories that shared linguistic or cultural identities . For example , nationalist movements led to the unification of Italy in 1861 and Germany in 1871 . <p> In the 19th Century , the merging of nation and state became a global principle through anti-colonial movements . Colonised populations adopted the idea of national self-determination to demand independence from imperial rule . After World War II , dozens of new states emerged , and the nation-state became the dominant model of political organisation worldwide . <p> The alignment between a nation and a state is rarely complete . Many states contain multiple ethnic or linguistic groups , while some nations remain divided across several states . In the 21st Century , as nationalism resurges and global power balances political shifts , the idea of the nation-state continues to shape geopolitics , war , and competition over resources , markets , and identity . <p> The contemporary system of sovereign states is formally organised through institutions such as the United Nations , which enshrines legal equality between states and non-interference in the internal matters of a state . But beneath this legal architecture lies a more turbulent reality . States pursue raw material harvesting , particularly of energy and water , and holding of artefacts ( embodied energy ) from within and outside their territory , and also protect these endeavours with political influence and military security ( both of which require energy expenditure ) . In such a system , nationalism becomes both glue and fuel ; it binds populations together internally while sharpening distinctions externally . <p> Roots of Modern Nationalism <p> As empires fragmented and colonialism disintegrated in the 19th and 20th centuries , the territorial state became a worldwide model , and nationalism became a mobilising force against imperialism . In Asia , Africa , and Latin America , anti-colonial movements adopted the language of national self-determination . By the mid-20th Century , the nation-state had become the universal political unit . <p> In many regions , the state preceded the nation . Colonial borders in Africa and the Middle East enclosed diverse linguistic and ethnic communities within artificial frontiers . After independence , governments undertook nation-building through education , official languages , military service , political and military domination of minority populations in a state by majority populations , and shared historical narratives . Where these efforts succeeded , the nation-state stabilised . Where they faltered , internal divisions persisted . Today 's conflicts often reflect unresolved tensions between imposed territorial boundaries and evolving identities . <p> The Logic of the Nation-State in Capitalism <p> Despite globalisation , digital interconnection , and the growth of international institutions , the nation-state remains the primary actor in world politics . Its legitimacy rests on a collective identity that defines insiders and outsiders . Its security depends on territorial integrity . Its prosperity depends on access to finance , markets and technology , and resource control . <p> Nationalism 's resurgence is not an aberration but a structural feature of a system built on sovereign units . In times of uncertainty -- economic volatility , demographic change , technological disruption -- national identity offers stability and political clarity . Yet the same force can polarise societies and harden interstate rivalries . <p> The nation-state system has brought a measure of order through recognised borders and legal equality , but it has also institutionalised rivalry . As power diffuses and global challenges intensify , the interplay between sovereignty and interdependence will determine whether the 21st Century is defined more by global cooperation or conflict . <p> GEOPOLITICS <p> Under capitalism , geopolitics is about control over natural resources , renewable and non-renewable , e.g. , water , energy , rare earths , etc , and markets . Religious and ethnic differences also play a role , but that is a subject that will not be discussed in this paper . <p> Control of Natural Resources <p> Control over natural resources has long shaped international disputes and conflicts . Water is a critical resource . River basins that cross national borders are potential flashpoints . Dams and upstream diversions can alter downstream livelihoods , transforming hydrological disputes into diplomatic crises . As climate change intensifies droughts and variability , water governance will become more politically charged . <p> In the 21st Century , competition increasingly focuses on critical minerals necessary for digital technologies and renewable energy systems . Lithium , cobalt , nickel , and rare earths are essential for batteries , electric vehicles , and advanced electronics . Control over these supply chains enhances economic and strategic resilience . While outright wars over such minerals have not occurred yet , states have used trade restrictions , investment controls , and diplomatic pressure to secure access to critical minerals . <p> Markets and Economic Access <p> Access to markets is a motive for expansion and conflict . Colonial empires sought not only territory but also captive markets for manufactured goods . Industrial competition in the late 19th and early 20th centuries heightened rivalry among European powers and contributed to the conditions that culminated in global war . <p> In the contemporary era , geoeconomics often substitutes for direct conquest . Sanctions , export controls , and trade agreements function as instruments of statecraft . Economic coercion allows states to pursue strategic objectives . However , when economic measures fail , war is possible . <p> The competition between the US and China demonstrates how market access , technological supremacy , and supply chain control are central to modern rivalry . Tariffs , restrictions on semiconductor exports , and scrutiny of foreign investment reflect a shift from pure economic globalisation toward strategic economic nationalism . <p> Multipolar Competition in the 21st Century <p> The post -- Cold War period is marked by the relative dominance of the United States . However , the rapid rise of China , to a lesser extent , India , and the assertive re-emergence of Russia have ushered in a more multipolar environment . Trump 's tariff war against the rest of the world and its wanting to annex Canada and Greenland are attempts to reassert US dominance . <p> The conflict between Russia and Ukraine is not solely about territory , but reflects competing visions of political alignment , historical identity , and regional order , and underlying them all , the US desire to undermine Russia 's primacy as a major global energy supplier . Ukraine 's assertion of independent nationhood challenges Moscow 's conception of historical unity and strategic buffer zones against NATO 's relentless expansion in the last few decades . The result is a war that blends geopolitical calculation with deeply rooted identity claims . <p> In the Indo-Pacific , tensions between China and the United States revolve around maritime dominance , technological leadership , and the political status of Taiwan . Here , economic interdependence coexists with strategic rivalry . Semiconductor supply chains , artificial intelligence development , and naval presence in contested waters represent both economic and security stakes . <p> Influence of the US Dollar and Multinational Corporations <p> The 2003 invasion of Iraq is linked to the strategic importance of oil and the global financial system centred on the U.S. dollar . Because most international oil trade is priced in dollars -- often called the " petrodollar system " -- the stability of dollar-based energy markets is closely tied to U.S. economic power . Iraq possesses some of the largest oil reserves in the world , and control over oil production and pricing can influence global energy markets . Critics of the war argue that maintaining influence over major oil-producing regions helps sustain the dominance of the dollar and the global financial system built around it . Geopolitical interventions in oil-rich regions can be understood partly as attempts to preserve the economic architecture that supports U.S. financial and strategic influence . <p> A somewhat different but related dynamic can be seen in the political crisis in Venezuela , which holds the world 's largest proven oil reserves . Over the past two decades , Chinese state-linked companies and banks became deeply involved in Venezuela 's oil sector through loans , investments , and long-term supply agreements . China has extended billions of dollars in credit to Venezuela in exchange for future oil deliveries , making it one of the country 's most important economic partners . This growing Chinese presence in Venezuela 's energy industry has been viewed by some policymakers in Washington as a strategic challenge , especially because it expands China 's influence in a region traditionally considered within the United States ' sphere of influence . During Venezuela 's political crisis in 2019 , the United States recognized opposition leader Juan Guaid ? as interim president and imposed sanctions on the country 's state-owned oil company PDVSA , which is the main source of national revenue . <p> More recently , developments in Venezuela have continued to highlight the centrality of oil to geopolitical calculations . After intense U.S. pressure and sanctions targeting the oil sector , the United States intervened in the political situation and captured Venezuelan President Nicol ? s Maduro on 3 January 2026 , an action widely interpreted as linked to the country 's vast energy resources and the strategic importance of controlling their production and export . Some analysts argue that these actions reflect broader geopolitical competition over energy resources and market access , especially given that China has been a major importer of Venezuelan oil and a key financial partner . Control over such resources affects not only energy markets but also the broader balance of economic influence among global powers . <p> These cases illustrate a broader phenomenon described as crony capitalism , where political power and corporate interests become closely intertwined . In crony capitalist systems , major economic decisions -- such as access to natural resources , infrastructure contracts , or financial privileges -- are shaped not purely by market forces but by political relationships between governments and powerful corporations . In the global energy sector , this can manifest as close ties between governments , multinational oil companies , financial institutions , and political elites . Critics argue that such relationships can encourage foreign interventions , sanctions regimes , or political pressure aimed at securing favourable conditions for specific corporate or national economic interests . Conflicts over oil and energy resources frequently reflect not only geopolitical rivalry but also the interaction between state power and corporate influence in the global economy . <p> Oil has been the single most strategically important commodity in modern history . It reshaped the production of goods and services , transport , warfare , and became deeply intertwined with economic development , national power and geopolitics . From the early days of the oil rush in Pennsylvania in the latter half of the 19th Century to the rise of multinational oil companies and the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries ( OPEC ) , to the present day , oil has been a central force in global politics . <p> Oil had an intimate relationship with state power . By the late 19th Century , governments began to recognise that access to secure oil supplies was essential for military strength and industrial growth . In the early 20th century , oil replaced coal as the dominant strategic fuel , especially for navies and mechanised armies . This shift transformed energy from a commercial commodity into a national security imperative , linking oil fields and sea lanes to imperial ambition and global rivalry . <p> The balance of power shifted dramatically in the mid-20th Century as oil-producing countries in the Middle East renegotiated concessions and eventually nationalised assets . The formation of OPEC marked a turning point , giving producing nations collective leverage over global markets and demonstrating how resource control could translate into geopolitical influence . <p> After the 1973 Yom Kippur War between the Arabs and Israel , several Arab oil-producing states imposed an oil embargo on countries that supported Israel . The resulting oil supply shock caused soaring prices and economic recession . This event revealed the vulnerability of industrial economies to energy disruption and fundamentally reshaped energy policy , strategic reserves , and international relations . <p> Oil has been both a driver of economic development and prosperity and a source of conflict . It fuelled wars , underpinned alliances , empowered corporations and states , and repeatedly redrawn the geopolitical map . Control over energy resources -- more than ideology alone -- has determined the contours of modern global power . <p> Energy has played a critical role in wars . As First Lord of the Admiralty of the British Navy in 1911 , Churchill realised that war was imminent with Germany . He recognised the strategic need to switch the Royal Navy from coal to oil for greater speed and efficiency . Churchill then secured oil from new oil finds in Persia . In 1914 , he spearheaded an agreement where the British government purchased a 51% controlling stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company to secure a reliable supply for the Navy . <p> In 1942 , the German Army made a major , high-stakes effort to seize the Baku oil field to sustain their war effort . Despite intense fighting in the Caucasus and reaching as far as Grozny , they were eventually forced to retreat following the Stalingrad disaster . <p> Imperial Japan had no fossil fuel reserves of its own , so it invaded fossil fuel-rich areas until it was defeated in World War II . In 1931 , it colonised Manchuria in Northeast China for its rich coal fields . After bombing Pearl Harbour in 1941 , Japan invaded Indonesia , and not Singapore , as Indonesia had coal and gas . Toward the end of World War II , Japan experienced severe shortages of aviation fuel , leading it to use pine oil ( turpentine ) . Simultaneously , they formalised kamikaze tactics as a desperation measure to compensate for a lack of trained pilots , fuel for training , and to allow them to inflict damage with minimal oil resources . <p> Energy remains central to economic growth , geopolitical stability , and national security . Energy transitions are slow , complex , and shaped as much by politics and technology as by markets . <p> As energy demand surges in emerging economies -- especially in China and India -- energy security becomes a strategic concern . Access to oil and gas reserves , pipeline routes , and maritime chokepoints influences foreign policy decisions . Energy interdependence can both stabilise and destabilise relations : it creates mutual reliance , but also vulnerability to disruption . <p> In the last few decades , advances in hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling unlocked vast reserves of oil and gas previously considered uneconomical . This technological breakthrough transformed the United States from a declining producer into one of the world 's largest energy producers , reshaping global markets and reducing U.S. dependence on Middle Eastern imports . Innovation can dramatically alter geopolitical calculations . <p> The 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan triggered a global reassessment of nuclear energy policy , leading some countries to scale back or reconsider nuclear programs . Public perception , safety concerns , and political reaction can redirect the trajectory of energy development . <p> The global energy system is in transition . Fossil fuels will remain significant for decades , even as renewable energy expands . Energy security , technological innovation , environmental pressures , and geopolitical competition are deeply intertwined -- and managing this complex interplay will define the future of the world . <p> At its core , geopolitics is about the control , organisation , and transformation of energy , and its use in production systems that transform raw materials into finished goods and services . Military power rests on industrial capacity . Financial systems depend on energy flows . Technological supremacy requires global logistics networks . <p> The relative stability that followed the end of the Cold War -- characterised by economic globalisation , institutional multilateralism , and the predominance of the United States -- has given way to a far more fragmented and contested landscape . The rise of China , the assertive geopolitical posture of Russia and the war in Ukraine , the increasing strategic weight of India , and the growing economic rise of middle powers -- the EU , Japan , Canada , Australia , Brazil , South Africa and Indonesia , instability in the Middle East , tensions in the Indo-Pacific are deeply rooted in questions of energy access , industrial production , and market control . <p> The domains of competition now include not only land , sea , and air but also cyberspace , outer space , semiconductor fabrication facilities , rare earth processing plants , undersea cables , social media platforms , and artificial intelligence systems , all of which draw heavily from the use of energy , other raw materials and technology . <p> The present geopolitical condition can be described as competitive multipolarity embedded within persistent interdependence . Major powers compete intensely , but their economies remain intertwined . Regional conflicts erupt , yet global financial systems continue to function . States seek autonomy and resilience , but they can not fully detach from global networks without incurring severe costs . <p> The US and China : Energy , Production Systems , and the Structure of Rivalry <p> At the heart of contemporary geopolitics is the relationship between the United States and China . Although this rivalry is often framed as a military or ideological conflict , its more fundamental roots are in energy systems , industrial production , and control of key technological supply chains . Modern geopolitical power depends on the ability to mobilise large energy flows and transform them into industrial output , technological progress , and military strength . <p> China 's rise over the past four decades has been driven by an extraordinary expansion of industrial production powered primarily by coal-based electricity and supported by integration into global markets . Large-scale energy availability enabled China to become the world 's manufacturing centre . Export-oriented industrialisation allowed China to accumulate capital , build infrastructure , and develop technological capabilities . Over time , the country moved up the industrial value chain from labour-intensive manufacturing toward advanced sectors such as electronics , telecommunications equipment , renewable energy technologies , and digital platforms . Today , China is the largest producer of solar panels , wind turbines , and electric vehicles , and it dominates the processing of rare earth minerals essential to modern electronics and energy technologies . <p> This transformation illustrates a central principle of geopolitical economy : industrial power follows energy availability . China 's massive coal reserves , combined with the rapid expansion of electricity generation capacity , provided the energetic foundation for its manufacturing expansion . At the same time , China became increasingly dependent on imported oil and natural gas to sustain transport systems , petrochemicals , and industrial activity . As a result , securing energy supplies became a major strategic priority . Long-term supply contracts , overseas investments in energy infrastructure , and maritime security policies reflect the importance of ensuring continuous energy flows to the Chinese economy . <p> The United States , by contrast , developed as an industrial superpower during the 20th Century based on abundant domestic fossil fuel resources , technological innovation , and large-scale industrial production . Although the United States experienced partial deindustrialisation in certain manufacturing sectors during the late 20th and early 21st centuries , it retains leadership in advanced technological fields such as semiconductor design , aerospace , artificial intelligence research , and digital platforms . Its financial system , anchored by the global role of the dollar , also remains central to global markets . <p> Energy continues to play a critical role in sustaining American geopolitical influence . The rapid expansion of shale oil and gas production transformed the United States into one of the world 's largest energy producers and exporters . In particular , the growth of liquefied natural gas exports has strengthened ties between the United States and energy-importing allies in Europe and Asia , providing an alternative to supplies from other major producers . Energy exports thus function not only as commercial transactions but also as instruments of geopolitical influence . <p> The rivalry between the United States and China is about control over critical segments of the global production system . Leadership in battery manufacturing , semiconductor fabrication , artificial intelligence infrastructure , telecommunications equipment , and aerospace technologies translates into both economic productivity and military capability . These sectors depend on complex supply chains linking energy extraction , mineral processing , industrial manufacturing , and technological innovation . <p> Unlike the Cold War confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union , the U.S. -- China relationship is characterised by profound economic interdependence . Global supply chains connect firms and industries across both economies . Multinational corporations manufacture products in China for global markets while relying on American technology , financial services , and consumer demand . Financial markets remain deeply integrated . This interdependence complicates strategic competition , because aggressive decoupling would impose high costs on both sides and disrupt global production networks . <p> At the same time , governments in both countries increasingly view supply chain resilience and technological autonomy as strategic priorities . The United States has introduced export controls restricting China 's access to advanced semiconductor technologies and chip-manufacturing equipment . China has responded by investing heavily in domestic semiconductor production , artificial intelligence development , and research capacity in emerging technologies such as quantum computing and advanced telecommunications infrastructure . <p> Energy systems intersect with this competition in multiple ways . The transition toward renewable energy technologies -- solar panels , wind turbines , batteries , and electric vehicles -- creates new arenas of industrial rivalry . China 's dominance in renewable energy manufacturing reflects large-scale investment , integrated supply chains , and control over key mineral processing industries . The United States and its allies are attempting to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and diversify supply chains to reduce dependence on Chinese production . <p> Geography also plays a role in shaping the rivalry . Maritime trade routes in the Indo-Pacific carry a large share of global energy and commodity flows . China 's dependence on imported oil transported through narrow sea lanes heightens its concern with maritime security and regional stability . Meanwhile , American alliances and naval presence in the region reinforce its role as a guarantor of maritime trade routes . <p> The Taiwan Strait represents the most dangerous flashpoint within this broader rivalry . The strategic importance of Taiwan extends far beyond politics . Taiwan hosts some of the world 's most advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities , producing chips essential for global electronics , computing systems , artificial intelligence , and advanced weapons platforms . A disruption to Taiwan 's semiconductor production would ripple across the entire global economy , affecting industries from automobiles and telecommunications to aerospace and defence . The island , therefore , represents a critical node in the global production system , making any conflict there a potential economic shock of unprecedented scale . <p> Ultimately , the rivalry between the United States and China is best understood as a contest over the organisation of the global energy -- industrial system . Energy availability enables industrial production ; industrial capacity enables technological innovation ; and technological leadership confers economic and military advantage . Control over supply chains , production technologies , and energy infrastructure , therefore , becomes a central objective of state strategy . <p> The outcome of this rivalry will help determine the structure of the global economy in the coming decades . Whether the world moves toward deeper fragmentation of production networks or manages to maintain a degree of cooperative interdependence will depend largely on how the United States and China navigate this complex interplay of energy systems , industrial power , and geopolitical ambition . <p> Russia , Ukraine , and the Energy Restructuring of Europe <p> Russia 's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 represents one of the clearest demonstrations of how energy systems and markets can become instruments of geopolitical power . In the decades preceding the conflict , Russia had become one of the world 's largest exporters of oil , natural gas , and coal , and a particularly dominant supplier of piped gas to Europe . This energy relationship formed a central pillar of the economic interdependence between Russia and Europe . When the war began , the disruption of these flows triggered one of the largest reorganisations of global energy markets in recent history . <p> Before 2022 , many European countries depended heavily on Russian natural gas transported through an extensive network of pipelines crossing Eastern Europe and the Baltic region . Russian energy exports not only generated large revenues for the Russian state but also gave Moscow considerable geopolitical leverage over energy-importing countries . The invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent sanctions imposed by Western governments fundamentally altered this relationship . Sanctions targeted Russian financial institutions , restricted access to advanced technology , and imposed limits on energy trade . In response , Europe moved rapidly to reduce dependence on Russian pipeline gas . <p> The adjustment required a dramatic restructuring of Europe 's energy supply system . Liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) imports increased sharply as European states turned to alternative suppliers , including shipments from the United States and other exporting countries . New LNG terminals were constructed or expanded , and pipeline infrastructure was reconfigured to enable energy flows from different sources . At the same time , European governments accelerated the deployment of renewable energy technologies such as wind and solar power to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels . Nuclear energy , previously in decline in several countries , re-emerged in policy debates as governments reconsidered the importance of stable , domestically produced electricity . <p> These changes reveal how energy systems shape geopolitical relationships . Russia 's ability to supply large quantities of natural gas had previously created economic interdependence that some policymakers believed would stabilise political relations . The war demonstrated the opposite possibility : energy dependence can create vulnerability when political relations deteriorate . By reducing its reliance on Russian gas , Europe sought to transform that vulnerability into a more diversified and resilient energy structure . <p> For Russia , the consequences were equally significant . Sanctions and declining European demand forced the country to redirect energy exports toward alternative markets , particularly in Asia . Oil shipments were rerouted through longer maritime routes , and new trade relationships developed with countries willing to purchase discounted Russian energy . This redirection of trade flows altered the geography of global energy markets and strengthened Russia 's economic ties with countries outside the Western sanctions regime , including China and other emerging economies . <p> The war also demonstrated how energy markets transmit geopolitical shocks across the global economy . Disruptions to Russian oil and gas exports caused price volatility in international energy markets . Because energy is a key input in transportation , manufacturing , and agriculture , rising energy prices cascaded through supply chains . Fertiliser production , which depends heavily on natural gas , became more expensive , contributing to higher food prices . Grain exports from the Black Sea region were also disrupted by the conflict , further intensifying pressure on the global food market . <p> Beyond its economic consequences , the war has reshaped Europe 's strategic landscape . The conflict has evolved into a prolonged war of attrition characterised by extensive use of drones , long-range missiles , trench fortifications , and cyber operations . Western governments have provided substantial military and financial assistance to Ukraine while maintaining economic sanctions against Russia . These developments have reinforced the importance of collective defence arrangements within the NATO alliance , which has expanded its membership and strengthened its presence along its eastern frontier . <p> European defence spending has increased significantly as governments reassess security risks in light of the war . The concept of European strategic autonomy -- once discussed primarily in terms of diplomatic independence -- has increasingly been linked to industrial capacity , technological capability , and energy security . Energy infrastructure , supply chains for military equipment , and domestic industrial production are now viewed as essential components of national and regional security . <p> Energy politics , therefore , sits at the centre of the conflict 's geopolitical consequences . The disruption of Russian energy exports forced Europe to reconsider its energy strategy , accelerate the transition toward renewable energy sources , and diversify supply chains . At the same time , Russia has attempted to reposition itself within global markets by strengthening economic relationships with non-Western partners and by adapting export routes to circumvent sanctions . <p> The broader lesson of the Russia -- Ukraine war is that energy markets are not merely economic mechanisms but strategic systems capable of transmitting geopolitical power . Control over energy resources and transportation routes can generate political leverage , while dependence on external suppliers can create strategic vulnerability . When conflicts disrupt these systems , the effects extend far beyond the battlefield , influencing inflation , trade flows , industrial production , and financial stability across the global economy . <p> In this sense , the war represents not only a military confrontation but also a major episode in the ongoing reorganisation of the global energy system . Europe 's shift away from Russian energy , Russia 's reorientation toward alternative markets , and the acceleration of renewable energy deployment all reflect the ways in which geopolitical conflict can reshape the structure of global energy production and trade . <p> The conflict demonstrates that energy remains one of the most powerful forces shaping international politics , linking war , markets , and industrial systems into a single geopolitical dynamic . <p> The Middle East : Energy , Conflict , and Strategic Realignment <p> The Middle East occupies a central position in global geopolitics largely because of its role in the world 's energy system . The region contains some of the largest proven reserves of oil and natural gas and has long functioned as a primary supplier of energy to global markets . Revenues from hydrocarbon exports finance state budgets , sovereign wealth funds , infrastructure development , and geopolitical initiatives across the region . As a result , political stability in the Middle East is closely linked to the functioning of international energy markets . Conflicts in the region carry consequences far beyond local politics , affecting global trade flows , commodity prices , and economic stability . <p> Oil production decisions by major exporters such as Saudi Arabia continue to influence global energy prices . Through coordination within production alliances , regional producers can adjust supply levels and thereby affect market conditions . This capacity gives energy-exporting states significant geopolitical leverage , as fluctuations in oil prices influence inflation , government revenues , and economic performance across the world . In this sense , the Middle East functions as one of the key nodes in the global energy system . <p> At the same time , the region remains one of the most politically volatile areas of the international system . The ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas has generated severe humanitarian consequences and heightened fears of wider regional escalation involving Iran and other actors . While the immediate conflict is geographically concentrated , its effects extend far beyond the battlefield because the Middle East lies astride some of the most important energy transportation routes in the world . <p> Shipping disruptions in the Red Sea have demonstrated how even localised conflict can influence global markets . A significant portion of global trade -- including energy shipments -- passes through maritime corridors connecting the Persian Gulf , the Red Sea , and the Mediterranean . When insecurity increases along these routes , shipping costs rise and global supply chains experience delays . Energy markets are particularly sensitive to such disruptions because oil and liquefied natural gas shipments depend heavily on secure maritime transportation . Consequently , regional conflicts can quickly translate into volatility in global commodity prices . <p> The economic and political importance of hydrocarbons has also shaped the strategies of the region 's major states . Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have accumulated enormous financial resources through decades of oil exports . These revenues are increasingly being used to finance long-term economic diversification strategies designed to prepare for a future in which fossil fuel demand may gradually decline . Investments in renewable energy , logistics infrastructure , digital technology , tourism , and global financial assets are intended to transform hydrocarbon wealth into broader economic investments . <p> Energy-exporting states are increasingly pursuing strategies of strategic hedging in response to the emerging multipolar order . While maintaining long-standing security relationships with the United States , many Gulf states are expanding economic and technological partnerships with China and other emerging powers . This diversification of external relationships reflects a pragmatic approach to geopolitics in which economic opportunities and market access take precedence over rigid ideological alignments . <p> Tensions involving Israel , Iran , and various non-state actors create persistent uncertainty that can affect market confidence and investment decisions . Energy infrastructure , shipping routes , and production facilities are all potential targets in regional confrontations . Even when direct damage to energy production is limited , the perception of risk can influence global oil prices and insurance costs for maritime transport . <p> Despite these challenges , many governments in the region are attempting to reposition their economies for the long term . Renewable energy projects are increasingly prominent in national development plans . These initiatives reflect recognition that the global energy transition may gradually reshape the geopolitical importance of fossil fuels . By investing in new energy technologies and diversified industries , Gulf states hope to remain central players in the evolving global energy system . <p> The geopolitics of the Middle East is part of the broader global effort to control energy resources , manage energy markets , and adapt national economies to an evolving energy landscape . The region remains both a major supplier of energy to the world and a focal point where the interaction of energy , finance , and geopolitics continues to shape the structure of the global economy . <p> Other Wars after World War II <p> Many wars have been fought since the end of World War II . A list of major inter-state wars , without comment , is given below : <p> The technological revolution reshapes geopolitics at every level . Artificial intelligence accelerates economic productivity while introducing military applications such as autonomous weapons , advanced surveillance , and cyberattacks that target infrastructure , elections , and financial systems . Space has become militarised , with satellites underpinning communication , navigation , and reconnaissance . <p> Control over data , algorithms , and digital infrastructure is as consequential as control over territory . Semiconductor fabrication plants become strategic assets . Undersea cables become vulnerable . Social media platforms become arenas of influence operations . <p> Climate Change , Energy Transition , and the Reorganisation of Global Production <p> Climate change is increasingly reshaping geopolitics not only through environmental impacts but also through the transformation of energy systems and industrial production . Rising temperatures , extreme weather events , and ecological stress act as multipliers of existing geopolitical tensions . Floods , droughts , and heatwaves damage infrastructure , disrupt transportation networks , and interrupt industrial supply chains . Agricultural production becomes more volatile , affecting global food markets and increasing the risk of political instability in vulnerable regions . Climate-driven migration further intensifies social and political pressures , particularly in regions already facing economic or environmental stress . <p> Beyond these immediate effects , climate change is catalysing a profound restructuring of global energy systems and industrial production . Efforts to limit greenhouse gas emissions require a transition away from fossil fuels toward electrification , renewable energy , and new industrial processes . This transformation is forcing governments and industries to reconfigure the technological and infrastructural foundations of modern economies . Electrification of transportation , large-scale deployment of renewable electricity , decarbonisation of heavy industries such as steel and cement , and modernisation of electricity grids all demand massive investment in new technologies and infrastructure . <p> Because these transformations affect the core of industrial production , climate policy has effectively become a form of industrial policy . Governments are competing to develop domestic manufacturing capacity in sectors such as solar panels , wind turbines , batteries , electric vehicles , and advanced energy storage systems . Countries that establish leadership in these technologies gain not only environmental benefits but also economic advantages through exports , technological innovation , and industrial employment . As a result , the transition to low-carbon energy systems is generating a new arena of geopolitical competition centred on control of emerging green industries . <p> At the same time , the energy transition is altering patterns of resource dependence . Reducing reliance on fossil fuels diminishes the strategic importance of traditional oil and gas exporters , but it simultaneously increases demand for minerals essential to renewable technologies . Lithium , cobalt , nickel , copper , and rare earth elements are required for batteries , electric motors , wind turbines , and other components of the low-carbon economy . This shift transfers geopolitical attention from hydrocarbon reserves to mineral deposits and the industrial processes required to refine and manufacture these materials into usable technologies . <p> Consequently , the geopolitical hierarchy of energy resources is being reorganised rather than eliminated . Countries that control critical mineral supplies or dominate processing and manufacturing capabilities gain strategic influence in the emerging energy system . The transition to renewable energy , therefore , does not remove the geopolitical significance of energy resources ; instead , it relocates it within new supply chains and industrial sectors . <p> Climate change also affects geopolitical dynamics through its impact on geography . Melting Arctic ice is gradually opening new maritime routes and increasing access to previously inaccessible natural resources . This development intensifies strategic competition among Arctic states seeking to secure shipping lanes , resource claims , and military presence in the region . At the same time , rising sea levels and extreme weather events threaten coastal infrastructure and densely populated urban regions , creating new security challenges for many countries . <p> Another dimension of climate geopolitics lies in disputes over responsibility and financial support . Developing countries , which often face the most severe climate impacts despite contributing relatively little to historical emissions , are demanding greater financial assistance for adaptation and mitigation efforts . Negotiations over climate finance , technology transfer , and development pathways have therefore become major points of contention between industrialised and developing nations . These debates reflect deeper questions about economic equity and the distribution of the costs associated with global decarbonisation . <p> The transformation of energy systems also interacts with global production networks . Manufacturing supply chains must adapt to new materials , technologies , and energy sources . Industries that depend heavily on fossil fuels are being pressured to adopt alternative energy inputs and more efficient production processes . In sectors such as steel , cement , chemicals , and transportation , the development of low-carbon production methods requires extensive technological innovation and capital investment . <p> As a result , the transition to a low-carbon economy is reshaping global industrial geography . Countries capable of combining technological innovation , access to critical minerals , and large-scale manufacturing capacity are likely to become leaders in the emerging energy system . Others may struggle to adapt if they remain dependent on fossil fuel exports or lack the industrial infrastructure required to participate in new energy technologies . <p> In this sense , climate change is not merely an environmental issue but a catalyst for a broader reconfiguration of economic and geopolitical power . The shift from fossil fuel -- based energy systems to renewable and electrified technologies is reorganising supply chains , altering patterns of resource dependence , and reshaping global production networks . Countries that successfully adapt their industrial systems to this new energy landscape will gain economic and strategic advantages , while those that fail to do so may find themselves marginalised in the emerging global order . <p> ENERGY AND NON-RENEWABLE MINERALS CRISES <p> Peak oil refers to the point at which the production of oil reaches its maximum rate and then begins to decline . Oil production follows a bell-shaped curve : production rises as new fields are discovered and developed , peaks when roughly half the resource has been extracted , and then declines as remaining reserves become harder and more expensive to exploit . Oil production will become increasingly difficult and costly after half of the original oil reserves are extracted . This can lead to economic and geopolitical stresses because modern transport , agriculture , and industry depend heavily on petroleum . <p> Reliable statistics for shale oil and gas are not available . At current rates of use of fossil fuels and uranium ore , fossil fuels and uranium ore will be exhausted by the end of this century . <p> Current energy use of 15 Gtoe is growing at 2% pa .
